Twelve doctor appointments.

Two MRIs, one CT scan, countless X-rays.

And not a single doctor thought to ask me one simple question.

The question that would have explained everything.

The question that took me YEARS to figure out. 

========

I'm 54. And for the past three years, I've been fighting a hip pain that no one could properly diagnose. 

And honestly? I was starting to think I was losing my mind.

It started small. Just this stabbing ache on the outside of my hip after my morning walks. The kind of thing you brush off. Slept wrong. Need new shoes. Finally feeling my age.

But it didn't go away. It got worse.

The pain started waking me up at night. I'd lie on my left side and within minutes, this deep burning pressure would build.

Like someone slowly pressing their thumb into the bone, harder and harder until I couldn't take it anymore. I'd flip to my right side. Twenty minutes later, same thing. Flip again. Left side. Right side. Stare at the ceiling. Try my back. 

My husband started calling me a rotisserie chicken.

I laughed the first few times. By month four, I wanted to throw my pillow at his head.

========

Here's what no one tells you about chronic pain: 

It's not just the pain. It's everything the pain takes from you.

By month six, I was averaging maybe three hours of broken sleep. I'd drag myself out of bed feeling like I'd aged twenty years overnight — this deep stiffness that took a full ten minutes of shuffling around the bedroom before I could walk normally. 

Stairs became something I had to psych myself up for. That shooting ache down my outer thigh with every single step. I started planning my whole day around avoiding them.

I stopped going to my Thursday morning yoga class. Cancelled on my sister's birthday dinner. Skipped my nephew's soccer games because the metal bleachers were agony and standing on the sidelines wasn't much better.

I was becoming the woman who always had a reason she couldn't come.

That wasn't who I was. I used to be the one organizing things. Dragging everyone out for hikes. First one on the dance floor at weddings, last one to leave. I once walked nine miles through Rome in a single day just because I didn't want to miss anything.

Now I was the one people had learned to stop inviting.

========

And the nights... God, the nights were the worst.

I'd lie there in the dark, brain spinning out of control, convinced something was seriously wrong. Bone cancer. A tumor. Some degenerative disease quietly eating away at my hip socket while doctors kept telling me everything looked "normal." I'd catastrophize for hours while the pain pulsed and my husband slept peacefully six inches away.

One night — maybe month eight or nine, I'd stopped keeping track by then — he rolled over and put his arm around me. This thing he's done for twenty-three years of marriage. His hand rested on my hip, gentle, half-asleep.

And I flinched. Pulled away. Couldn't help it. Even that soft pressure was too much.

He didn't say anything. But I saw his face in the glow of the alarm clock.

I still think about that look.

We don't really touch anymore. Not like we used to. And I can't tell if it's because I've pulled away so many times he's stopped trying, or because I've started preemptively angling my body away from him in bed, protecting that hip like it's made of glass.

Probably both.

========

That was the week I finally went to my doctor.

She pressed on my hip, asked if it hurt here (yes), here (god yes), and here (I nearly levitated off the table). She nodded like she'd solved a puzzle.

"Bursitis. Pretty common at your age. Take ibuprofen, ice it, should calm down in a few weeks."

It didn't.

Two months later, I was back. She referred me to an orthopedist.

He squinted at my X-rays for maybe sixty seconds while I sat there in that paper gown, feeling like a specimen.

"Some arthritis. Normal wear and tear. You're what, mid-fifties?" He said it like that explained everything. "We can try cortisone if the ibuprofen isn't cutting it."

The first injection actually helped. For about three weeks, I felt almost normal. Slept on my side two nights in a row. Started making plans again.

Then it came back. Worse somehow.

Second injection lasted maybe ten days. Third one might as well have been saline.

I went to another orthopedist — paid $400 out of pocket because supposedly he was "the best." Same answer. Arthritis. Wear and tear. "Have you considered physical therapy?"

So I tried it. Twice a week for two months. Clamshells, bridges, resistance bands, stretches that were supposed to "strengthen the stabilizers."

But every night, the pain was the same. Sometimes worse — there were days after PT when I could barely make it up my front steps.

When I told my therapist it wasn't helping, she looked almost hurt. "You have to trust the process."

I stopped going after ten weeks. Couldn't justify the copays for something that wasn't working.

Here's the thing about pain that doesn't show up on tests: doctors start looking at you differently.

You can see it. The slight skepticism. The barely-hidden impatience. The unspoken suggestion that maybe you're exaggerating. 

One doctor asked if I'd "considered talking to someone." Took me a second to realize he meant a therapist.

I drove home and sat in my car in the driveway for twenty minutes, engine off, just staring at my garage door. Wondering if this was just my life now. Wondering if I really was being dramatic. Wondering if everyone was right and I just needed to accept that this is what fifty-four feels like.

Wondering how many more years of this I could actually survive.

That was my lowest point.

========

Here's what I need you to understand about those three years and twelve appointments:

Every single doctor asked me the same questions.

Where does it hurt? How long has it been going on? Does it radiate? Any numbness or tingling? What makes it worse? What makes it better? Any injuries? What's your activity level? Family history of arthritis?

They asked about my weight. My exercise habits. My stress levels. Whether I'd tried yoga. Whether I'd tried losing weight. Whether I'd tried "just resting it."

But not ONE of them — not my GP, not the orthopedists, not the physical therapist, not the rheumatologist — asked me the question that actually mattered:

When did this start relative to my menopause?

It never even occurred to me to connect the two. Why would it?

Everyone warns you about the hot flashes. The night sweats. The mood swings. The brain fog. The weight that suddenly clings to your midsection no matter what you eat.

But hip pain that feels like someone's driving a railroad spike into your outer thigh every time you try to sleep on your side?

Nobody mentions that. It's not in any of the menopause pamphlets. Your gynecologist doesn't bring it up. Your friends complain about hot flashes over wine — nobody's talking about their hips.

So I never made the connection.

Until 2:47 AM on a Tuesday.

I remember the exact time because I'd been watching the clock for hours. 

I was scrolling through my phone because sleep wasn't coming and I needed something to do besides lie there counting the ways my body had failed me.

And I found this video from a menopause researcher.

I almost kept scrolling. I'd watched dozens of videos by then. Read hundreds of articles. Tried every stretch, every supplement, every sleeping position anyone had ever suggested. None of them told me anything useful.

But something made me click. Maybe it was the 2 AM desperation. Maybe I was just too tired to keep scrolling. Maybe some part of me wasn't ready to give up yet.

Whatever it was, I'm grateful for it every single day.

Because about two minutes in, this researcher asked a question that made my whole body go still.

"Did your pain start around or after menopause?"

I paused the video.

Sat up in bed. Hip screaming at the sudden movement, but I barely noticed.

Did it?

I thought back. When did I first start waking up stiff? When did stairs first become a thing I noticed? When did I first feel that weird ache after a long walk?

And I realized: it was about eight months after my periods stopped completely. Right around the time I'd finally accepted that menopause was "over" and I could stop thinking about it.

I'd never connected those two things.

In three years of doctors and tests and failed treatments, I'd never once thought: wait. This started right after menopause. Is that a coincidence?

And nobody — not a single medical professional — had ever suggested it might not be.

I pressed play.

About what's actually happening inside the hip during and after menopause.

But I know this:

If you've been fighting hip pain that doesn't show up on X-rays...

If you've started wondering whether you're just being dramatic, whether this is just "getting older," whether you should just accept it and stop complaining...

I don't want that for you.

Twelve doctor appointments.

Two MRIs, one CT scan, countless X-rays.

And not a single doctor thought to ask me one simple question.

The question that would have explained everything.

The question that took me YEARS to figure out. 

========

I'm 54. And for the past three years, I've been fighting a hip pain that no one could properly diagnose. 

And honestly? I was starting to think I was losing my mind.

It started small. Just this stabbing ache on the outside of my hip after my morning walks. The kind of thing you brush off. Slept wrong. Need new shoes. Finally feeling my age.

But it didn't go away. It got worse.

The pain started waking me up at night. I'd lie on my left side and within minutes, this deep burning pressure would build.

Like someone slowly pressing their thumb into the bone, harder and harder until I couldn't take it anymore. I'd flip to my right side. Twenty minutes later, same thing. Flip again. Left side. Right side. Stare at the ceiling. Try my back. 

My husband started calling me a rotisserie chicken.

I laughed the first few times. By month four, I wanted to throw my pillow at his head.

========

Here's what no one tells you about chronic pain: 

It's not just the pain. It's everything the pain takes from you.

By month six, I was averaging maybe three hours of broken sleep. I'd drag myself out of bed feeling like I'd aged twenty years overnight — this deep stiffness that took a full ten minutes of shuffling around the bedroom before I could walk normally. 

Stairs became something I had to psych myself up for. That shooting ache down my outer thigh with every single step. I started planning my whole day around avoiding them.

I stopped going to my Thursday morning yoga class. Cancelled on my sister's birthday dinner. Skipped my nephew's soccer games because the metal bleachers were agony and standing on the sidelines wasn't much better.

I was becoming the woman who always had a reason she couldn't come.

That wasn't who I was. I used to be the one organizing things. Dragging everyone out for hikes. First one on the dance floor at weddings, last one to leave. I once walked nine miles through Rome in a single day just because I didn't want to miss anything.

Now I was the one people had learned to stop inviting.

========

And the nights... God, the nights were the worst.

I'd lie there in the dark, brain spinning out of control, convinced something was seriously wrong. Bone cancer. A tumor. Some degenerative disease quietly eating away at my hip socket while doctors kept telling me everything looked "normal." I'd catastrophize for hours while the pain pulsed and my husband slept peacefully six inches away.

One night — maybe month eight or nine, I'd stopped keeping track by then — he rolled over and put his arm around me. This thing he's done for twenty-three years of marriage. His hand rested on my hip, gentle, half-asleep.

And I flinched. Pulled away. Couldn't help it. Even that soft pressure was too much.

He didn't say anything. But I saw his face in the glow of the alarm clock.

I still think about that look.

We don't really touch anymore. Not like we used to. And I can't tell if it's because I've pulled away so many times he's stopped trying, or because I've started preemptively angling my body away from him in bed, protecting that hip like it's made of glass.

Probably both.

========

That was the week I finally went to my doctor.

She pressed on my hip, asked if it hurt here (yes), here (god yes), and here (I nearly levitated off the table). She nodded like she'd solved a puzzle.

"Bursitis. Pretty common at your age. Take ibuprofen, ice it, should calm down in a few weeks."

It didn't.

Two months later, I was back. She referred me to an orthopedist.

He squinted at my X-rays for maybe sixty seconds while I sat there in that paper gown, feeling like a specimen.

"Some arthritis. Normal wear and tear. You're what, mid-fifties?" He said it like that explained everything. "We can try cortisone if the ibuprofen isn't cutting it."

The first injection actually helped. For about three weeks, I felt almost normal. Slept on my side two nights in a row. Started making plans again.

Then it came back. Worse somehow.

Second injection lasted maybe ten days. Third one might as well have been saline.

I went to another orthopedist — paid $400 out of pocket because supposedly he was "the best." Same answer. Arthritis. Wear and tear. "Have you considered physical therapy?"

So I tried it. Twice a week for two months. Clamshells, bridges, resistance bands, stretches that were supposed to "strengthen the stabilizers."

But every night, the pain was the same. Sometimes worse — there were days after PT when I could barely make it up my front steps.

When I told my therapist it wasn't helping, she looked almost hurt. "You have to trust the process."

I stopped going after ten weeks. Couldn't justify the copays for something that wasn't working.

Here's the thing about pain that doesn't show up on tests: doctors start looking at you differently.

You can see it. The slight skepticism. The barely-hidden impatience. The unspoken suggestion that maybe you're exaggerating. 

One doctor asked if I'd "considered talking to someone." Took me a second to realize he meant a therapist.

I drove home and sat in my car in the driveway for twenty minutes, engine off, just staring at my garage door. Wondering if this was just my life now. Wondering if I really was being dramatic. Wondering if everyone was right and I just needed to accept that this is what fifty-four feels like.

Wondering how many more years of this I could actually survive.

That was my lowest point.

========

Here's what I need you to understand about those three years and twelve appointments:

Every single doctor asked me the same questions.

Where does it hurt? How long has it been going on? Does it radiate? Any numbness or tingling? What makes it worse? What makes it better? Any injuries? What's your activity level? Family history of arthritis?

They asked about my weight. My exercise habits. My stress levels. Whether I'd tried yoga. Whether I'd tried losing weight. Whether I'd tried "just resting it."

But not ONE of them — not my GP, not the orthopedists, not the physical therapist, not the rheumatologist — asked me the question that actually mattered:

When did this start relative to my menopause?

It never even occurred to me to connect the two. Why would it?

Everyone warns you about the hot flashes. The night sweats. The mood swings. The brain fog. The weight that suddenly clings to your midsection no matter what you eat.

But hip pain that feels like someone's driving a railroad spike into your outer thigh every time you try to sleep on your side?

Nobody mentions that. It's not in any of the menopause pamphlets. Your gynecologist doesn't bring it up. Your friends complain about hot flashes over wine — nobody's talking about their hips.

So I never made the connection.

Until 2:47 AM on a Tuesday.

I remember the exact time because I'd been watching the clock for hours. 

I was scrolling through my phone because sleep wasn't coming and I needed something to do besides lie there counting the ways my body had failed me.

And I found this video from a menopause researcher.

I almost kept scrolling. I'd watched dozens of videos by then. Read hundreds of articles. Tried every stretch, every supplement, every sleeping position anyone had ever suggested. None of them told me anything useful.

But something made me click. Maybe it was the 2 AM desperation. Maybe I was just too tired to keep scrolling. Maybe some part of me wasn't ready to give up yet.

Whatever it was, I'm grateful for it every single day.

I paused the video.

Sat up in bed. Hip screaming at the sudden movement, but I barely noticed.

Did it?

I tried to remember. When did this really start? Not the bad pain — the early stuff. The first time I noticed something wasn't quite right.

I thought back. When did I first start waking up stiff? When did stairs first become a thing I noticed? When did I first feel that weird ache after a long walk?

And I realized: it was about eight months after my periods stopped completely. Right around the time I'd finally accepted that menopause was "over" and I could stop thinking about it.

I'd never connected those two things.

In three years of doctors and tests and failed treatments, I'd never once thought: wait. This started right after menopause. Is that a coincidence?

And nobody — not a single medical professional — had ever suggested it might not be.

I pressed play.

About what's actually happening inside the hip during and after menopause.

But I know this:

If you've been fighting hip pain that doesn't show up on X-rays...

If doctors keep calling it arthritis or bursitis while the treatments don't work...

If you've started wondering whether you're just being dramatic, whether this is just "getting older," whether you should just accept it and stop complaining...

Watch this video.

It's about ten minutes. It might be the first thing about your hip pain that actually makes sense.

I'm not saying that to sell you anything. I'm saying it because I spent three years in pain when I didn't have to. Three years of my life. Three years of sleep. Three years of slowly pulling away from my husband, my friends, myself.

I don't want that for you.

text:
For almost two years I have not slept a full night on my own side.

Here's what it actually looks like.

I lie down on my right side, and for a little while it's fine.

Then, slowly, that hip starts to ache - a deep, heavy pressure on the outside of the joint, like someone leaning the heel of their hand into the bone and pressing harder the longer I stay there.

So I roll to my left.

Twenty minutes later, the same thing starts on that side.

Onto my back.

Stare at the ceiling.

Back to the right.

My husband started calling me a rotisserie chicken, turning over and over all night long, and the first few times I even laughed.

By about month four I wanted to throw the pillow at his head.

So I did what everyone tells you to do: I blamed the bed.

I bought a new mattress.

Hundreds of dollars, and it changed nothing.

So I figured it was the pillows - got the fancy ones, then one of those long body pillows to put between my knees.

Nothing.

I tried the topper my sister swore by.

The mattress cover that's supposed to relieve pressure points.

I even slept in the guest room for a week thinking maybe it was my side of the bed.

The ache didn't care where I slept.

Because the bed, it turns out, was never the problem.

What no one tells you about not sleeping is that it isn't only about being tired.

It's what the exhaustion does to the rest of your life.

By month six I was running on maybe three or four broken hours a night.

I'd drag myself out of bed feeling like I'd aged twenty years overnight, and it took ten minutes of shuffling around the bedroom before I could walk like a normal person.

I was short with the people I love over nothing.

I stopped making morning plans because I never knew which version of me was going to wake up.

I started dreading my own bed - lying there with a knot in my stomach, already bracing for it.

I finally went to my doctor.

She pressed on the hip, asked if it hurt here (yes) and here (god yes), nodded, and said "bursitis, common at your age - try ibuprofen and sleep on your back." I can't sleep on my back.

Two months later a different doctor called it wear and tear, gave me a cortisone shot that helped for a few weeks and then faded, and suggested maybe I just needed to lose a little weight.

Not one of them - not the GP, not the orthopedist, not anyone - asked me the question that finally explained it: when did this start, relative to my menopause?

It never occurred to me to connect the two either.

Everyone warns you about the hot flashes and the night sweats.

Nobody mentions that you'll stop being able to lie on your own side.

It's not in the menopause pamphlets.

Your friends talk about their hot flashes; nobody's talking about their hips at 3 a.m. So I never made the connection.

I finally did one of those nights I was awake anyway, scrolling to have something to do besides lie there, when I found a video from a menopause specialist.

I almost kept scrolling, because it mentioned menopause and I didn't think that had anything to do with my hip.

But I was awake anyway, so I let it play.

A couple of minutes in, she explained exactly what happens inside the hip during menopause - why the ache lands in that one specific spot on the outside of the joint, and why lying on it at night hurts the way it does.

For the first time, it made sense.

It wasn't the mattress.

It wasn't how I was sleeping.

It wasn't my age.

And it wasn't in my head.

There was a real, physical reason this was happening, and just understanding it finally made me feel like I wasn't imagining it.

She also walked through a simple routine women are using to actually get relief - not to cover it up or work around it, but to rebuild what had been quietly breaking down.

I started doing it too, and it's the first thing in two years that's let me stay on one side long enough to fall asleep.

I won't promise it's your answer.

I don't know your body.

But if you flip from hip to hip all night like a rotisserie chicken, if you've bought every mattress and pillow and none of it touched the real thing, if you've started dreading your own bed and half-wondering whether it's all in your head, give it ten minutes.

I'll leave it right below - no email, no sign-up, just press play.

She explains the why better than I could at three in the morning.

Watch it tonight, before you buy one more pillow.
